title: Our Solar System
subtitle: Click a world. Learn what it is like.
note: Planets are shown bigger and closer together so you can see them. In real space they are much farther apart.

bodies.name: The Sun
bodies.headline: A star at the center of everything we know nearby.
facts: The Sun is a star — a giant ball of glowing hot gas.
It is so big that about one million Earths could fit inside it.
Almost every planet, moon, and space rock in our solar system goes around the Sun.
The Sun's light takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. That light keeps us warm.

bodies.name: Mercury
bodies.headline: The smallest planet, and the closest to the Sun.
facts: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest of the eight planets.
It has almost no air, so days are scorching hot and nights are freezing cold.
A year on Mercury (one trip around the Sun) takes only 88 Earth days.
A day on Mercury is longer than its year! It spins very slowly.

bodies.name: Venus
bodies.headline: Earth's twin in size — but a much hotter neighbor.
facts: Venus is almost the same size as Earth, so people call them twins.
It is the hottest planet. Thick clouds trap heat like a heavy blanket.
Venus spins the other way from most planets, and it spins very slowly.
A day on Venus is longer than its year.

bodies.name: Earth
bodies.headline: Our home — the only world we know with life.
facts: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only one we know has living things.
Most of Earth's surface is covered by oceans of liquid water.
Earth has one moon. The Moon's pull helps make ocean tides.
One trip around the Sun is one year: about 365 days.

bodies.name: The Moon
bodies.headline: Earth's closest neighbor in space.
facts: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. It goes around Earth, not the Sun by itself.
We always see the same face of the Moon from Earth because it spins at the same pace it orbits.
The Moon has no air to breathe and no liquid water on its surface.
Its gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and helps make high and low tides.

bodies.name: Mars
bodies.headline: The red planet, with ice at its poles.
facts: Mars looks rusty red because its soil has a lot of iron oxide — the same stuff as rust.
It is colder and drier than Earth, with a very thin atmosphere.
Mars has ice caps at its north and south poles.
A day on Mars is about 24 and a half hours — almost like ours.

bodies.name: Jupiter
bodies.headline: The giant of the solar system.
facts: Jupiter is the biggest planet. All the other planets could fit inside it with room to spare.
It is a gas giant — mostly hydrogen and helium, with no solid ground like Earth's.
The Great Red Spot is a huge storm that has lasted for hundreds of years.
Jupiter has dozens of moons. Four big ones were first seen by Galileo in 1610.

bodies.name: Saturn
bodies.headline: The planet with the brightest rings.
facts: Saturn is a gas giant, a little smaller than Jupiter, famous for its rings.
The rings are made of countless bits of ice and rock, from tiny grains to house-sized chunks.
Saturn is so light for its size that it would float in a giant bathtub of water.
It also has many moons. Titan, the largest, has a thick atmosphere.

bodies.name: Uranus
bodies.headline: An ice giant that rolls on its side.
facts: Uranus is an ice giant, farther out and much colder than Jupiter or Saturn.
It spins almost on its side, like a ball rolling around the Sun.
Its blue-green color comes from methane gas in its air.
A year on Uranus lasts 84 Earth years.

bodies.name: Neptune
bodies.headline: The farthest planet, with the fastest winds.
facts: Neptune is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun.
It is an ice giant, deep blue, and very cold.
Even so far from the Sun, Neptune has the fastest winds of any planet.
A year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years. One Neptune year is longer than a human life.

bodies.name: Pluto
bodies.headline: A dwarf planet at the edge of the neighborhood.
facts: Pluto used to be called the ninth planet. Today it is a dwarf planet.
It is smaller than Earth's Moon and very far from the Sun.
Pluto has a heart-shaped icy region and five known moons. The biggest moon is Charon.
Scientists still study Pluto. Being a dwarf planet does not make it less interesting!

belts.name: Asteroid Belt
belts.headline: A ring of space rocks between Mars and Jupiter.
facts: The asteroid belt is a region of leftover rocks between Mars and Jupiter.
Asteroids are leftover pieces from when the solar system formed.
They are far apart. Spaceships can fly through the belt without bumping into them.
Ceres, the largest object there, is also a dwarf planet.
